sourceCheck: Pinned GitLab 19.4 and GitLab Runner 19.4, both released on 2026-09-17, as confirmed by the [19.4 release notes](https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/19/gitlab-19-4-released/). The newest patch listed is [19.4.1, released 2026-09-23](https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-1-released/). GitLab 19.5 is not released: the [upcoming page](https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/upcoming/) identifies it as the next release. The [maintenance policy](https://docs.gitlab.com/policy/maintenance/) schedules monthly releases for the third Thursday, making the next scheduled date 2026-10-15. Opened the release index, the CI/CD portions of the 19.0–19.4 release notes and the deprecations overview. Attempted all three requested XML feeds, but the browsing tool rejected their XML content types; their contents could not be independently read. Release status was verified through the HTML pages instead. [Merged results pipelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/merged_results_pipelines/), [merge trains](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/merge_trains/), [protected environments](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/environments/protected_environments/) and [needs:project](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/#needsproject) show Tier: Premium, Ultimate. The downstream page's [Fetch artifacts from an upstream pipeline](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/downstream_pipelines/#fetch-artifacts-from-an-upstream-pipeline) also shows Tier: Premium, Ultimate; the YAML reference's needs:pipeline:job subsection has no separate Tier line. The [executor documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/runner/executors/) lists SSH, Shell, Parallels, VirtualBox and Custom in maintenance mode, and additionally includes Docker Machine marked deprecated in that subsection. The [YAML reference](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/#imagedocker) says image:docker works with Docker and Kubernetes executors. [CI/CD job tokens](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/jobs/ci_job_token/) default to JWT format since GitLab 19.0. New UI variables default to Masked visibility since GitLab 18.3 according to [CI/CD variables](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/variables/). The [merge request protected-resource section](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/merge_request_pipelines/#control-access-to-protected-variables-and-runners) permits protected variables and runners since 18.1 when the project setting enables access, both branches are protected in the same project, and the initiating user has push or merge access to the target branch; fork merge requests are excluded. [Cache key names](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/caching/#cache-key-names) assigns the -protected suffix to eligible protected-ref pipelines or pipelines initiated by a Maintainer or Owner; the role-based behavior dates from 18.4.5. The [deprecated keywords page](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/deprecated_keywords/) lists globally defined image, services, cache, before_script and after_script; only and except with refs, variables, changes and kubernetes variants; the publish keyword and pages job name; and environment:kubernetes:namespace and environment:kubernetes:flux_resource_path. Relevant deprecated keywords remain usable. No requested baseline topic was found removed; the maintenance-mode list has the Docker Machine nuance above. Histories, tiers, offerings and statuses were checked for the selected facts. Excluded post-19.4 behavior, including merge-request-title skip directives, needs:pipeline:job optional and the new cache:key:files limit; excluded Beta, Experiment and disabled-by-default features. Successfully opened these paths on docs.gitlab.com: /releases/, /releases/upcoming/, /policy/maintenance/, /releases/19/gitlab-19-0-released/, /releases/19/gitlab-19-1-released/, /releases/19/gitlab-19-2-released/, /releases/19/gitlab-19-3-released/, /releases/19/gitlab-19-4-released/, /releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-1-released/, /update/deprecations/, /ci/yaml/, /ci/yaml/deprecated_keywords/, /ci/jobs/, /ci/pipelines/, /ci/quick_start/, /ci/jobs/job_control/, /ci/jobs/job_rules/, /ci/yaml/workflow/, /ci/yaml/needs/, /ci/variables/, /ci/variables/predefined_variables/, /ci/variables/where_variables_can_be_used/, /ci/pipelines/settings/, /ci/pipelines/schedules/, /ci/jobs/ci_job_token/, /ci/jobs/fine_grained_permissions/, /ci/secrets/id_token_authentication/, /user/project/repository/branches/protected/, /ci/runners/runners_scope/, /ci/runners/configure_runners/, /ci/runners/new_creation_workflow/, /ci/runners/hosted_runners/linux/, /runner/, /runner/executors/, /runner/register/, /ci/caching/, /ci/jobs/job_artifacts/, /ci/yaml/artifacts_reports/, /ci/environments/, /ci/environments/protected_environments/, /ci/environments/deployment_safety/, /ci/resource_groups/, /ci/pipelines/merge_request_pipelines/, /ci/pipelines/merged_results_pipelines/, /ci/pipelines/merge_trains/, /ci/pipelines/downstream_pipelines/, /ci/pipelines/pipeline_architectures/, /ci/yaml/includes/, /ci/yaml/yaml_optimization/, /ci/components/, /ci/inputs/, /ci/yaml/script/, /ci/jobs/job_execution/, /ci/yaml/lint/, /ci/pipeline_editor/ and /runner/configuration/advanced-configuration/. Feed attempts: /releases/releases.xml, /releases/patch-releases.xml and /releases/breaking-changes.xml.

cards.statement: GitLab uses the order of YAML keywords in `.gitlab-ci.yml` to schedule jobs.
cards.explanation: YAML mapping key order does not schedule jobs; configuration keywords define the execution order.
cards.misconception: YAML keyword order determines execution order.

cards.statement: GitLab appends `default:before_script` commands to a job's own `before_script` commands.
cards.explanation: A job's own `before_script` replaces the corresponding default value instead of combining with it.
cards.misconception: Default commands merge with commands defined by a job.

cards.statement: GitLab passes global `default` keywords from a parent pipeline into its child pipeline.
cards.explanation: Global job defaults stay within their pipeline. A downstream pipeline uses its own configuration defaults.
cards.misconception: Downstream pipelines inherit the upstream pipeline's global job defaults.

cards.statement: A job can use `inherit:variables` to select the top-level variables it receives.
cards.explanation: A list under `inherit:variables` preserves the named defaults and excludes the other top-level variables.

cards.statement: Omitting `stages` gives a pipeline `.pre`, `build`, `test`, `deploy` and `.post`.
cards.explanation: When top-level `stages` is omitted, GitLab supplies `.pre`, `build`, `test`, `deploy` and `.post` in that order.

cards.statement: A job that omits `stage` joins the first stage listed in the pipeline's `stages` array.
cards.explanation: GitLab assigns a job that omits `stage` to `test`, regardless of which stage appears first.
cards.misconception: An unspecified job stage means the first configured stage.

cards.statement: Jobs assigned to the same stage can execute concurrently when runners are available.
cards.explanation: Jobs in one stage share an execution level, so available runners can execute them concurrently.

cards.statement: By default, GitLab cancels running jobs in a stage when another job in that stage fails.
cards.explanation: Running jobs in the current stage continue after a peer fails under the default failure behavior.
cards.misconception: One stage failure immediately cancels its running peer jobs.

cards.statement: A pipeline containing just `.pre` and `.post` jobs runs those jobs in their stage order.
cards.explanation: A pipeline needs at least one job in a stage other than `.pre` or `.post` to run.
cards.misconception: The special boundary stages form a runnable pipeline on their own.

cards.statement: A job name beginning with a dot makes its configuration available as a hidden template.
cards.explanation: GitLab skips execution of jobs whose names start with a dot while retaining their configuration for reuse.

cards.statement: GitLab reserves `stages` as a configuration keyword when developers choose job names.
cards.explanation: A job named `stages` conflicts with a reserved keyword and is invalid as a job definition.

cards.statement: CI Lint validates CI/CD configuration supplied through `include` in `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
cards.explanation: CI Lint checks included configuration as part of its syntax validation.

cards.statement: GitLab Runner runs `before_script` and `script` in one shell for each job.
cards.explanation: The runner combines these sections, so shell state from `before_script` remains available in `script`.

cards.statement: A job's `after_script` commands can read variables that its `script` commands export.
cards.explanation: GitLab Runner starts `after_script` in a separate shell; variables exported in `script` do not carry over.
cards.misconception: after_script continues in script's shell context.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 17.0, canceling a job during `script` starts its configured `after_script`.
cards.explanation: Normal cancellation runs the cleanup section before the job reaches its final canceled state.

cards.statement: An `after_script` failure changes the job to failed after its `script` succeeds.
cards.explanation: An `after_script` failure does not change the job's exit code or a successful main script's outcome.
cards.misconception: Cleanup failure overrides the successful main script result.

cards.statement: GitLab runs a job's `after_script` after a failure classified as `script_failure`.
cards.explanation: After a job failure, GitLab runs `after_script` for `script_failure`, rather than other failure types.

cards.statement: A failed job with `allow_failure: true` triggers later jobs that use `when: on_failure`.
cards.explanation: Allowed failures count as successful when GitLab decides whether later `on_failure` jobs should run.
cards.misconception: Any failed job activates on_failure jobs, including allowed failures.

cards.statement: With `allow_failure:exit_codes` set, GitLab treats other failing exit codes as ordinary failures.
cards.explanation: The configured list selects allowed failures; failing exit codes outside it retain normal failure handling.

cards.statement: `retry:when` and `retry:exit_codes` combine as an AND condition for automatic job retries.
cards.explanation: GitLab retries when either the configured failure type or a listed exit code matches, within the `retry:max` budget.
cards.misconception: Both the failure-type filter and exit-code filter need to match before GitLab retries.

cards.statement: A job's `timeout` value takes precedence over a shorter maximum timeout set on its runner.
cards.explanation: The runner's maximum job timeout caps execution even when the job requests a longer timeout.
cards.misconception: A YAML job timeout overrides the runner's maximum timeout.

cards.statement: In conservative mode, a started `script` job with `interruptible: false` blocks new-commit auto-cancel.
cards.explanation: In conservative mode, a started script job with `interruptible: false` keeps its pipeline running when a newer pipeline starts for the same ref.

cards.statement: `workflow:auto_cancel:on_job_failure: all` confines cancellation to the failing job's stage.
cards.explanation: `workflow:auto_cancel:on_job_failure: all` cancels the pipeline and its running jobs across stages.
cards.misconception: Failure auto-cancel affects the failing stage instead of the whole pipeline.

cards.statement: `parallel:matrix` creates job instances with different combinations of CI/CD variable values.
cards.explanation: GitLab expands the configured matrix combinations into separate instances of the job.

cards.statement: `needs` lets a test job start while unrelated build jobs are still running.
cards.explanation: GitLab schedules the consumer after its listed producers finish instead of waiting for their whole stage.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

cards.statement: `needs: []` makes GitLab wait for the previous stage before starting a job.
cards.explanation: An empty `needs` list schedules the job as soon as GitLab creates the pipeline.
cards.misconception: An empty needs list restores ordinary stage ordering.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

cards.statement: GitLab accepts a job's `needs` dependency on a producer assigned to the same pipeline stage.
cards.explanation: GitLab accepts explicit dependencies between jobs in the same stage.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

cards.statement: `needs` on a parallel job lets its consumer start when the first instance succeeds.
cards.explanation: A plain dependency on a parallel job waits for every instance of that producer.
cards.misconception: Any successful parallel instance satisfies a plain needs dependency.

cards.statement: `needs:parallel:matrix` selects specific combinations from a producer matrix job.
cards.explanation: GitLab waits for the producer instances identified by the configured matrix identifiers and values.

cards.statement: A job with `needs` downloads artifacts from each completed job in earlier stages.
cards.explanation: A job using `needs` restricts artifact downloads to the producers named in its dependency list.
cards.misconception: Adding needs retains the ordinary broad artifact downloads.

cards.statement: A `needs` entry with `artifacts: false` keeps the dependency while skipping its artifacts.
cards.explanation: A `needs` entry keeps its scheduling dependency when `artifacts: false` disables the producer's artifact download.

cards.statement: GitLab can create a pipeline when `rules` exclude a job named in a required `needs` entry.
cards.explanation: A missing required producer prevents pipeline creation. Mark a potentially absent producer with `needs:optional`.
cards.misconception: GitLab silently ignores required dependencies on excluded jobs.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

cards.statement: A matching `rules:needs` adds its jobs to the job-level `needs` list.
cards.explanation: `rules:needs` in a matching rule replaces the job's entire `needs` configuration.
cards.misconception: Rule-level needs extend the existing dependency list.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, `needs:project` waits for an active upstream pipeline to finish.
cards.explanation: `needs:project` fetches the specified job's latest successful artifacts for that ref while another pipeline may run.
cards.misconception: Cross-project artifact retrieval waits for the running upstream pipeline.

cards.statement: `needs:pipeline` copies the latest pipeline status from another project's default branch.
cards.explanation: GitLab mirrors the upstream default-branch pipeline's status onto the configured job.

cards.statement: The pipeline graph groups jobs by `needs` when developers select its dependency view.
cards.explanation: The dependency view arranges the graph according to relationships between jobs.

cards.statement: GitLab lets later matching job rules change attributes set by an earlier matching rule.
cards.explanation: GitLab stops evaluating a job's `rules` at the first match and uses that rule's attributes.
cards.misconception: Later matches override earlier matching rules.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

cards.statement: A rule containing `if`, `changes` and `exists` matches when each condition succeeds.
cards.explanation: GitLab combines the conditions within one rule with AND logic.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

cards.statement: `rules:when: manual` gives a job `allow_failure: true` by default.
cards.explanation: A manual job defined inside `rules` defaults to `allow_failure: false`.
cards.misconception: Manual jobs have the same allow_failure default inside and outside rules.

cards.statement: A matched rule's `when` value overrides the job-level `when` value for that job.
cards.explanation: GitLab applies the matching rule's scheduling choice when both locations specify `when`.

cards.statement: `rules:variables` can assign a job variable when the associated condition matches.
cards.explanation: `rules:variables` supplies variable values to the job when that rule matches.

cards.statement: A job's `interruptible` setting can override a matching `rules:interruptible` value.
cards.explanation: The matching rule's `interruptible` value takes precedence over the job-level setting.
cards.misconception: Job-level interruptible outranks a matching rule's setting.

cards.statement: `rules:if` supports RE2 syntax when GitLab compares a variable to a regular expression.
cards.explanation: GitLab evaluates regular expression comparisons using RE2 syntax.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

cards.statement: `rules:if` matches a slash-delimited variable on the right of `=~` as literal text.
cards.explanation: GitLab treats a valid slash-delimited pattern held in the right-hand variable as a regular expression.
cards.misconception: Regex operators treat variable-held patterns as literal strings.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

cards.statement: `rules:changes` in a scheduled pipeline checks differences from the previous commit by default.
cards.explanation: Scheduled pipelines lack a push event, so `rules:changes` is true unless `compare_to` defines a comparison.
cards.misconception: Scheduled pipelines compare against the preceding commit automatically.

cards.statement: `rules:changes` uses the target branch as its comparison base in merge request pipelines.
cards.explanation: GitLab compares the merge request's listed file paths against its target branch.

cards.statement: Job-level `rules:exists` searches the pipeline's own project and ref by default.
cards.explanation: GitLab checks the listed paths in that project and ref unless the rule specifies another project.

cards.statement: GitLab adds jobs using its implicit default filters to merge request pipelines.
cards.explanation: Jobs that omit `rules`, `only` and `except` default to branch and tag pipelines, excluding merge request pipelines.
cards.misconception: Default job selection includes merge request pipelines.
